Rally Ledger

Tennis shots & errors, point by point. On which shot do players hit winners or make unforced errors?

About the analysis

How the analysis works

Counting shots

Chartists record who serves, which strokes follow and who wins the point. The timing chart counts the final attempt by default. Turn off “Count the final miss” to count only the legal serve and successful strokes. A first-serve fault adds nothing. We check the last hitter against the server and point winner before assigning a winner or an error.

At Wimbledon in 2023, Djokovic’s winners averaged shot 5.72 and his unforced errors shot 6.06. Exclude the miss and his error average drops to 5.06. The point-by-point table always shows completed shots.

One match or several?

In Match view, each measured winner counts once in the winner average. In Player and Head-to-head, each game with a measured winner counts once. We repeat the calculation for unforced errors. A game can qualify for one average, both or neither.

Say you hit one winner on shot 8 in the first game. In the next, you hit three winners, each on shot 4. Give each game equal weight and you get 6 shots per winner, halfway between 8 and 4. Give each winner equal weight and you get 5, the average of 8, 4, 4 and 4. Go a third game without a winner and both lengths stay the same. Your four winners now work out to 1.33 per game.

Checking the count

We remove duplicate points and set aside matches with conflicting point records or unclear game numbers. We test serve faults, missed returns and who hit the last shot. You can check the 2023 Wimbledon men’s final in Match view. Its 334 charted points include 53 Alcaraz winners and 55 Alcaraz unforced errors.

Limitations

Explore Tennis Point Stages to see where in the exchange points are decided.

Coverage. Volunteers choose which matches to chart. Some rivalries have missing meetings, and some charts stop before match point. A matched result confirms the winner and final score. It cannot verify that every point was charted. Check how many matches and endings a figure covers.

Judgment calls. Chartists can disagree about whether an opponent forced a miss. A point with an unclear ending still counts toward the game’s total points. We need a known ending and rally length to use it in either length average.

Tactics. Winning most long rallies in a match gives you little reason on its own to prolong the next one. Check who served in those rallies. Across matches, consider the opponent and court surface.

Definitions
Winner
A shot that wins the point outright, such as a forehand down the line that passes the opponent untouched. We count aces separately.
Forced and unforced errors
On a forced error, the chartist judges that the opponent’s shot caused the miss. On an unforced error, the player misses a ball the chartist considers playable.
Last shot attempted
The shot number on which the point ended. A miss on shot five counts as the fifth attempt.
Shots in play
Count the legal serve as shot one. A winner on shot five counts as five shots in play. A miss on the same attempt leaves four.
Endings per game
Divide the player’s endings of one kind by all charted games, including service games, return games and tiebreaks.
Game-average share
Find the percentage of points in each game that ended with the player’s winner or, for the error statistic, their unforced error. Average those percentages.
Pearson’s r
A measure of how two averages vary together across matches. Near +1, longer winner rallies tend to go with longer error rallies. Near −1, longer winner rallies tend to go with shorter error rallies. Near zero, there’s little linear relationship.
Zero and a dash
Zero is a result. A dash means there isn’t enough data or variation to calculate a value.
Sources and code

Jeff Sackmann and the volunteers at Tennis Abstract’s Match Charting Project compiled the men’s and women’s point records. See the coverage notes for the match chartist’s name when available.
